pages.title: Formula One
pages.extract:
Formula One or F1 is the premier category of Motor sport, with cars racing at over 350 kph. They mostly race on purpose-built circuits but sometimes on closed streets, with Monaco the most famous example.
Each F1 racetrack is different, with its own mix of straights, tight bends and chicanes. It’s a much sterner test of driving skill than the oval tracks used in other racing categories, where the simpler corners and long straights favour brute engine power. F1 tracks are 4-5 km long and the race is over enough laps to total 305 km. Cars usually make one or two pit stops to change tyres, but they may not re-fuel.
Grand Prix or GP is the series of F1 races over a year, with winners totting up points towards the World Championship. "Grand Prix" means big prize and these are the most lucrative racing events, drawing the best cars and drivers plus huge crowds. That term might also translate as huge price, as only manufacturers with deep pockets can afford to develop such cars, field teams and transport them continually around the world. Barely a dozen can do so.
Formula One races are sometimes held outside the Grand Prix calendar, but these are more modest events, and from the traveller’s point of view F1 and GP are much the same.

pages.title: Fort William
pages.extract:
Fort William is a town at the foot of  the Great Glen, on the west coast of the Scottish Highlands. It's the main transport, commercial and visitor hub for the area: its attractions include Ben Nevis, Nevis Range ski resort, the Caledonian Canal, and "The Jacobite" steam train. 
The town in 2021 had a population of 5630. A couple of miles north is a secondary built-up area, with the villages of Inverlochy, Caol, Bannavie and Corpach totalling another 5000 population; their facilities are also described on this page.

pages.title: Kunitachi
pages.extract: Kunitachi (国立市 Kunitachi-shi) is a city in western Tokyo. The naming of Kunitachi comes from its location: sandwiched between Kokubunji (国分寺) and Tachikawa (立川), the first kanji in each city was combined to create a new name.

pages.title: Port St Johns
pages.extract:
Port St Johns is a town on the Wild Coast of South Africa.
Renowned worldwide for its open beaches, awesome weather and wild waters, Port St Johns and the Wild Coast offer visitors to South Africa an opportunity to experience unspoiled Africa.
Visitors to the small town of Port St Johns will encounter an eclectic mix of local characters and African flair. The friendly chaos of this bustling coastal community is inviting and mesmerizing.  Many visitors describe their experiences here as “distinctly African”; striking a balance between the changing face of rural South Africa and traditional recognition of the past.

pages.title: Taal
pages.description: municipality of the Philippines in the province of Batangas
pages.extract:
Taal is a municipality in Batangas. The old downtown (Poblacion) is noted for its Spanish colonial architecture, and is designated as a National Historical Landmark by the Philippine government.
Being about a two-hour drive from Metro Manila, Taal is an easy getaway from the concrete jungle and chaos there, a much closer alternative to the better-known heritage town Vigan. There are many tourist-oriented businesses; you may find a heritage house with a cafe or a bed and breakfast in it. Even the 7-Eleven store near the basilica is built in colonial-style architecture to blend with the surroundings.
Taal is just across a small river from the larger town of Lemery. Most of Taal, including the downtown, is inland on higher ground to the southeast, but Butong barangay is along the coast south of Lemery and has some beach resorts.
